summary: Source-based expansion of scheme and stack foundations from the Stacks Project, Bhatt–Scholze and de Jong. SF.0: fibre products by gluing and the Zariski representability criterion, relative Spec, and the named morphism classes with base change. SF.1: faithfully flat descent of modules via the Amitsur complex, fpqc descent of quasi-coherent sheaves and affine morphisms, and statement-level algebraic spaces, the bootstrap theorem, quotient stacks and Keel–Mori. SF.2: independence of quasi-coherent cohomology from the topology, the pro-étale versus étale comparisons including the left-completion theorem, and statement-level smooth/proper base change and Rf_!. SF.3: degree, genus and Riemann–Roch for Gorenstein proper curves, representability of the Picard scheme of a smooth projective curve and H¹_ét(μ_n) = Pic⁰[n]. SF.4: formal functions, Grothendieck existence and algebraization; flat deformations of modules and schemes; modifications, alterations, Lipman's resolution criterion and de Jong's alteration theorems. SF.5: proper pushforward and flat pullback on rational equivalence, the key formula, Gysin maps and Chern classes, intersection products with the moving lemma and projection formula. SF.6 was not read. Recorded gaps include the stage-order issue that Riemann–Roch for curves uses a Chow-homology lemma, and the absence of Hodge index, surface Riemann–Roch and the Frobenius-graph computation from the library.

nodes.title: Fibre products of schemes via gluing and the Zariski representability criterion
nodes.statement: The category of schemes has a final object Spec Z, products and fibre products (Stacks Lemma 26.16.1). The proof uses the representability criterion Lemma 26.15.4: a functor F on schemes is representable if it satisfies the sheaf property for the Zariski topology and has subfunctors F_i that are representable, representable by open immersions, and jointly cover F. For affine inputs the fibre product is Spec(A ⊗_R B) (Lemma 26.17.2). Gluing data of locally ringed spaces glue (Lemma 26.14.1), and if all pieces are schemes the result is a scheme (Lemma 26.14.2).
hypotheses: No hypotheses for existence.
Lemma 26.14.1 states the mapping properties of glued spaces with their proof omitted.
proofSteps: Spec Z is final (Lemma 26.6.4), so only fibre products are needed (Categories 4.18.4).
For X → S ← Y set F(T) = Mor(T, X) ×_{Mor(T, S)} Mor(T, Y) and verify Lemma 26.15.4; F is a Zariski sheaf by gluing morphisms with Lemma 26.14.1.

Subfunctors F_{i,j,k} come from affine opens U_i ⊂ S, V_j ⊂ f⁻¹U_i, W_k ⊂ g⁻¹U_i; each is representable by Lemma 26.6.7 (affine fibre products agree in schemes and locally ringed spaces), representable by open immersions via a⁻¹V_j ∩ b⁻¹W_k, and together they cover.

Lemma 26.15.4 itself: choose X_i representing F_i and opens U_{ij} where the universal element lies in F_j; the comparison maps are isomorphisms satisfying the cocycle condition; glue (Lemmas 26.14.1–26.14.2) and use the sheaf property to produce the universal element.
acceptance: Base-change diagrams identify every arrow (stage acceptance): record both projections and the induced maps.
Test: Spec(A ⊗_R B) for affine inputs, and a non-affine gluing of two affine lines along an open subscheme.

nodes.title: Separated, finitely presented, flat, smooth, étale and proper morphisms and base change
nodes.statement: Separated morphisms (Definition 26.21.3) are stable under base change (Lemma 26.21.12(3)). A morphism is of finite presentation if it is locally of finite presentation, quasi-compact and quasi-separated (Definition 29.21.1), stable under base change (Lemma 29.21.4). Flatness is defined at points of the source relative to the target (Definition 29.25.1) and is stable under base change (Lemma 29.25.8). Smooth morphisms (Definition 29.34.1) carry no separation or quasi-compactness hypotheses and are stable under base change (Lemma 29.34.5). A morphism is étale if it is étale at every point (Definition 29.36.1), stable under base change (Lemma 29.36.4). A morphism is proper if it is separated, of finite type and universally closed (Definition 29.41.1), stable under base change (Lemma 29.41.5).
hypotheses: Statement-level reading; proofs of the base-change lemmas were not decomposed.
No Stacks statement was found for the stage acceptance claim that a flat universal family cannot establish flatness of its parameter scheme.
proofSteps: Proofs not read in this pass; stability under base change is by the cited lemma in each case.
acceptance: State flatness, smoothness and properness as properties of named morphisms (stage text).

nodes.title: Descent of modules along faithfully flat ring maps (Amitsur complex)
nodes.statement: Let R → A be faithfully flat. For every R-module M the extended Amitsur cochain complex 0 → M → A ⊗_R M → A ⊗_R A ⊗_R M → ⋯ is exact (Stacks Lemma 35.3.6). Every descent datum (N, φ) for modules along R → A (Definition 35.3.1) is effective; M ↦ (A ⊗_R M, can) is an equivalence from R-modules to descent data; and its inverse is H⁰ of the associated cosimplicial module (Proposition 35.3.9). The source proves effectivity and omits the proofs of the other two statements.
hypotheses: R → A faithfully flat.
Omitted in the source: Lemma 35.3.3, degrees −1 and 0 of Lemma 35.3.6, and parts (2)–(3) of Proposition 35.3.9.
proofSteps: Lemma 35.3.2: the cocycle condition makes the relevant composite a projector that is an isomorphism.
Lemma 35.3.5: if R → A has a section, the complex is exact (Simplicial 14.28.4–14.28.6).
Lemma 35.3.6: exactness descends along faithfully flat R → R′; take R′ = A, where A → A ⊗_R A has a section, and apply Lemma 35.3.5.
Lemmas 35.3.7–35.3.8: a descent datum is effective iff A ⊗ H⁰ → N is an isomorphism, and effectivity descends along faithfully flat maps.

Proposition 35.3.9(1): reduce to R → A with a section σ; put M = {n : 1 ⊗ n = φ(n ⊗ 1)}; writing φ(n ⊗ 1) = Σ a_i ⊗ x_i gives n = Σ a_i x_i, and applying σ to the cocycle identity shows Σ σ(a_i)x_i ∈ M, proving surjectivity of A ⊗ M → N; injectivity follows by applying φ.
acceptance: Test: Z → Z_p × Z[1/p] is faithfully flat, and a module glued from compatible data over Z_p and Z[1/p] descends.
Flatness vocabulary is supplied by FoundationsAndLibraryIntegration LI.1.

nodes.title: fpqc descent of quasi-coherent sheaves and of affine morphisms
nodes.statement: For an fpqc covering {U_i → S} of a scheme, every descent datum on quasi-coherent sheaves is effective, and QCoh(S) → descent data is fully faithful (Proposition 35.5.2). Descent data (V_i/X_i, φ_{ij}) relative to an fpqc covering with each V_i → X_i affine are effective (Lemma 35.37.1); the same holds for closed immersions (Lemma 35.37.2) and quasi-affine morphisms (Lemma 35.38.1). Lemma 35.39.1 relates representability of a sheaf to effectivity of its descent datum, and remarks that the omission of fpqc there is deliberate.
hypotheses: fpqc coverings (Topologies Definition 34.9.1). Lemma 35.36.2, used to localize, applies to τ ∈ {fpqc, fppf, étale, smooth, syntomic} and classes P stable under base change and finite disjoint unions that are effective over surjective τ-maps of affines (statement only).
Full faithfulness uses Lemma 35.2.2, whose proof is omitted, and a final check in Proposition 35.5.2 is omitted.
proofSteps: Affine S with a standard covering: Γ(S, O) → Γ(∐ U_i, O) is faithfully flat (Lemma 35.5.1), so Proposition 35.3.9 applies.
General coverings: refine over an affine cover (Topologies 34.9.8, Definition 34.9.10) and glue (Lemma 35.2.4); faithfulness because a flat local ring map is faithfully flat (Algebra 10.39.17).

Lemma 35.37.1: affineness is local on the base and stable under base change (Morphisms 29.11.3, 29.11.9), so Lemma 35.36.2 reduces to one faithfully flat Spec A → Spec R; with V = Spec B, Proposition 35.3.9 gives C = Ker(B → A ⊗_R B) with A ⊗_R C ≅ B; C is closed under products because φ is an algebra map; U = Spec C descends V.
acceptance: Stage: effective descent for the required objects; the classes shown effective in the parts read are quasi-coherent modules, affine morphisms, closed immersions and quasi-affine morphisms.
Test: descent of an affine morphism along Spec A → Spec R faithfully flat.

nodes.title: Algebraic spaces, the bootstrap theorem, quotient stacks and Keel–Mori (statements)
nodes.statement: An algebraic space over S is an fppf sheaf F with representable diagonal and a surjective étale morphism from a scheme (Definition 65.6.1); the quotient U/R of a scheme by an étale equivalence relation is an algebraic space (Theorem 65.10.5). Bootstrap (Theorem 80.10.1): F is an algebraic space if it is a quotient U/R with s, t flat and locally of finite presentation and j an equivalence relation, or a sheaf with a surjective, flat, locally finitely presented cover by an algebraic space that is representable by algebraic spaces, or a sheaf with representable diagonal and such a cover. If G → B is flat and locally of finite presentation and acts freely on X, then X/G is an algebraic space and X is an fppf G-torsor over it (Lemma 80.11.7). Algebraic stacks (Definition 94.12.1) have diagonal representable by algebraic spaces, which is equivalent to Isom sheaves being algebraic spaces (Lemma 94.10.11). [U/R] is an algebraic stack for smooth groupoids (Theorem 94.17.3) and when s, t are flat and locally of finite presentation (Theorem 97.17.2); [B/G] is algebraic iff G is flat and locally of finite presentation (Lemma 97.18.3). Keel–Mori (Theorem 106.13.9): an algebraic stack with finite inertia I_X → X has a uniform categorical moduli space f: X → M with f separated, quasi-compact and a universal homeomorphism (Definition 106.12.1).
hypotheses: Statement-level reading: proofs of Theorems 80.10.1, 94.17.3, 97.17.2 and 106.13.9 and the definition of inertia were not read.

No standalone Stacks lemma stating that [X/G] is algebraic, and no main-text definition of coarse moduli space, were found; Stacks uses categorical moduli spaces (Definition 106.12.1) and coarse quotients (Definition 83.6.1).
proofSteps: Proofs not read in this pass. As recorded by the reader, Theorem 80.10.1 uses Lemma 80.5.3, and Keel–Mori uses Lemmas 106.13.4, 106.13.7 and 106.13.8.
acceptance: Separate a moduli functor from a stack and a coarse space from a fine moduli object (stage text): the Keel–Mori output is a uniform categorical moduli space, not a fine moduli space.
A quotient consumer must receive the universal property and the stabilizer (inertia) hypotheses explicitly; representability and properness are separate proofs (stage acceptance).

nodes.title: Cohomology of quasi-coherent modules is independent of the topology
nodes.statement: For a quasi-coherent O_S-module F and τ ∈ {Zariski, étale, smooth, syntomic, fppf}, H^q(S, F) = H^q((Sch/S)_τ, F^a) = H^q(S_Zar, F^a) = H^q(S_étale, F^a) (Stacks Proposition 35.9.3, restated as Étale Cohomology Theorem 59.22.4); fpqc is not included. Compatibility with pushforward holds only for quasi-compact quasi-separated morphisms on the small Zariski or étale sites (Proposition 35.9.4).
hypotheses: F quasi-coherent; τ among Zariski, étale, smooth, syntomic, fppf.
proofSteps: q = 0: F^a is a sheaf (Lemma 35.8.1, from Proposition 35.5.2 and Topologies 34.4.2, 34.5.2, 34.6.2, 34.7.2, 34.9.7).
Lemma 35.9.1 reduces to a single affine covering; Lemma 35.9.2 identifies the Čech complex with s((A/R)• ⊗ M), so higher Čech cohomology vanishes by Lemma 35.3.6.
Cohomology on Sites 21.10.9 gives vanishing of higher cohomology on affines; for separated U, 21.10.7 and Cohomology of Schemes 30.2.6 give the comparison.
General S: compare injective resolutions (Derived Categories 13.18.6) and the Čech spectral sequences over an affine cover, which agree on E₂.

Do not extend to the fpqc site or to non-quasi-coherent coefficients.

nodes.title: Pro-étale versus étale sheaves and derived categories (Bhatt–Scholze §§5.1–5.3)
nodes.statement: For a scheme X let X_proét be the site of weakly étale X-schemes with fpqc covers (Definition 4.1.1) and ν: Shv(X_proét) → Shv(X_ét). For an étale sheaf F, ν^*F is computed by colimits over presentations U = lim U_i (Lemma 5.1.1), and ν^* is fully faithful on sheaves with essential image described by this formula (Lemma 5.1.2). For bounded below K, K ≃ ν_*ν^*K (Corollary 5.1.6), so ν^*: D^+(X_ét) → D^+(X_proét) is fully faithful with described essential image (Proposition 5.2.6); if X_ét is locally of finite cohomological dimension, the statements extend to unbounded complexes (Remark 5.2.8). The subcategory D_cc(X_proét) of §5.3 is equivalent to the left completion of D(X_ét), via μ = R lim ν^* and γ = {ν_*τ^{≥−n}} (Proposition 5.3.2).
hypotheses: X any scheme (no qcqs hypothesis) in §5.1; abelian sheaves; bounded below in Proposition 5.2.6 unless X_ét is locally of finite cohomological dimension (Remark 5.2.8, stated with 'one can show').
Proposition 5.3.2 uses repleteness of X_proét (Propositions 4.2.8, 3.2.3(1)) and left completeness of replete topoi (Proposition 3.3.3), decomposed in EnhancedDerivedSheaves E2.
proofSteps: Lemma 5.1.1: the problem is local on X, so assume X affine; use ind-étale presentations (Remark 4.2.5), the sheaf criterion (Lemma 4.2.6), the fact that Zariski and étale covers come from some U_i, and filtered colimits.

Corollary 5.1.6: reduce to sheaves by a triangulated class closed under filtered colimits; it suffices that H^p(U, ν^*I) = 0 for injective I, where Čech cohomology suffices (SGA 4 V.4.3) and covers are cofinal by Theorem 2.3.4; conclude as filtered colimits are exact.
Proposition 5.2.6: follows formally from Corollary 5.1.6 together with Lemma 5.2.7 (a functor with a fully faithful adjoint is a Verdier quotient by its kernel).

Proposition 5.3.2: ν^* factors through the left completion by repleteness and Proposition 3.3.3; the bounded-below case is 5.2.6; K ∈ D_cc iff all truncations are; μ and γ are mutually inverse ('one can check').
acceptance: Coefficient level: these comparisons are for abelian sheaves; ℓ-adic and rational coefficients need Bhatt–Scholze §§5.5–6 (not read) (stage acceptance).
When D(X_ét) is not left-complete, the authors do not know an example separating their D′ from D_cc (p. 39).

nodes.title: Smooth and proper base change for torsion sheaves and Rf_! (statements)
nodes.statement: Smooth base change (Stacks Theorem 59.89.2): for a cartesian square with f smooth and g quasi-compact quasi-separated, base change holds in all degrees for abelian sheaves whose stalks at geometric points are torsion of orders invertible on S. Proper base change (Theorem 59.91.11): for f proper and any g, base change holds for abelian torsion sheaves, with no invertibility condition. For f separated of finite type with quasi-compact quasi-separated target, Rf_! = Rf̄_* ∘ j_! on bounded below complexes with torsion cohomology sheaves (or on all complexes for torsion Λ), independent of the compactification and compatible with base change (§63.9, Lemmas 63.9.1–63.9.4).
hypotheses: Torsion orders invertible on the base for smooth base change; torsion only for proper base change.
Proofs not read; compactification (More on Flatness 38.33.8) and Lemma 59.78.2 enter them.

nodes.title: Degree, genus and Riemann–Roch for Gorenstein proper curves
nodes.statement: For X proper over a field k of dimension at most 1, deg L = χ(L) − χ(O_X), and deg E = χ(E) − n·χ(O_X) for E locally free of rank n; the degree depends on the triple E/X/k (Definition 33.44.1) and is invariant under field extension (Lemma 33.44.2). X has a dualizing module ω_X = H⁻¹(ω•_X), coherent and Cohen–Macaulay, with Hom(F, ω_X) = Hom_k(H¹(X, F), k) for quasi-coherent F, and ω_X ≅ Ω_{X/k} if X is smooth of relative dimension 1 (Lemma 53.4.1). For X proper of dimension 1 with H⁰(X, O_X) = k, the (arithmetic) genus is g = dim_k H¹(X, O_X) (Definition 53.8.1). Riemann–Roch (Lemma 53.5.2): if X is proper over k, Gorenstein and equidimensional of dimension 1, then ω_X is invertible, deg ω_X = −2χ(O_X), χ(E) = deg E − ½·rank(E)·deg ω_X, and h^i(E) = h^{1−i}(E^∨ ⊗ ω_X). Hence deg ω_X = 2g − 2 (Lemma 53.8.3) and, for smooth X, h⁰(Ω) = g and deg Ω = 2g − 2 (Lemma 53.8.4). In genus 0 with H⁰ = k, degree-0 invertible modules are trivial, degree d > 0 gives h⁰ = d + 1 and a closed immersion into P^d, and Gorenstein genus-0 curves are plane conics (Lemmas 53.10.1–53.10.3).
hypotheses: Gorenstein and equidimensional of dimension 1 for Riemann–Roch; nonsingular (normal) curves are Gorenstein (Duality for Schemes 48.24.3).

Duality inputs (Duality for Schemes 48.24.2–48.24.4, Dualizing Complexes 47.20.2) were read as statements only; the proof uses Chow Homology Lemma 42.41.3, which belongs to stage SF.5 material (see gap).
proofSteps: Gorenstein implies Cohen–Macaulay (48.24.2), so ω_X is a dualizing module (Lemma 53.4.2) and is invertible (§48.24).
Apply (53.5.0.3) to ω_X; it combines Definition 33.44.1 with (53.5.0.2), which is Chow Homology Lemma 42.41.3: deg E = deg(c₁(E) ∩ [X]₁).
Lemma 53.5.1 gives χ(O_X) = −χ(ω_X), hence deg ω_X = −2χ(O_X).
Substitute back for general E; the symmetry of dimensions is Remark 53.4.3 (h⁰(L) = h¹(L⁻¹ ⊗ ω_X)).
acceptance: Genus zero: triviality of degree-0 line bundles and the conic embedding (Lemmas 53.10.1–53.10.3).
Genus one: no Stacks result beyond an example was found; the genus-one test needs another source.
Extension of scalars: degree and genus are invariant (Lemmas 33.44.2, 53.8.2).

nodes.title: Representability of the Picard scheme of a smooth projective curve and H¹_ét(μ_n)
nodes.statement: Let k be separably closed and X a smooth projective curve over k. The Picard functor Pic_{X/k}, the fppf sheafification of T ↦ Pic(X_T) (Definition 44.4.1), is representable (Proposition 44.6.6). Moreover Pic_{X/k} = ∐_d Pic^d with each Pic^d a g-dimensional smooth proper variety, Pic⁰ is an open and closed subgroup, γ_d: Hilb^d → Pic^d is surjective for d ≥ g and smooth for d ≥ 2g − 1, and Hilb^g → Pic^g is birational (Lemma 44.6.7). When H⁰ = k and a rational point exists, Pic(X) = Pic(X_{k′})^{Gal} (Lemma 44.7.1). For X smooth projective of genus g over an algebraically closed field and n invertible, H¹_ét(X, μ_n) = Pic⁰(X)[n] canonically, and this is non-canonically (Z/n)^{2g} (Lemma 59.69.1).
hypotheses: No section is assumed: a rational point exists because k is separably closed (Varieties 33.25.6). Proposition 44.3.6 and Definition 44.6.3 involve geometric irreducibility; the reader did not locate where the hypotheses of Proposition 44.6.6 supply it (not verified).
Lemma 59.69.1 uses Groupoids Proposition 39.9.11 (torsion of abelian varieties), which the source describes as a key fact without an elementary proof.
proofSteps: Choose a rational point σ; Lemma 44.6.1 feeds Lemma 44.4.3 (via Descent Proposition 35.5.2), giving the split exact sequence 0 → Pic(T) → Pic(X_T) → Pic_{X/k}(T) → 0, so Pic_{X/k} ≅ Pic_{X/k,σ}.

Apply the criterion Lemma 44.5.1 (from Schemes 26.15.4): the sheaf property from the proof of 44.4.3; the open subfunctor where Rf_{T*}L is invertible in degree 0 (Lemma 44.6.2, via Derived Categories of Schemes 36.32.3); this subfunctor is an open of Hilb^g (Lemma 44.6.4, via Proposition 44.3.6, Remark 44.3.7, 36.30.4 and deg L = g); translates cover (Lemma 44.6.5, via 30.17.1 and Varieties 33.43.8).
Lemma 59.69.1: Theorems 59.24.1 and 59.68.5, the Kummer sequence (59.28.1), Lemma 44.6.7 and Groupoids Proposition 39.9.11.
acceptance: The Stacks Project contains no identification of the Jacobian Tate module with degree-one étale cohomology with dual conventions, and does not name an Abel–Jacobi map; γ_d is the available map (stage acceptance cannot be met from this source).
Degree zero: Pic⁰ is open and closed (Lemma 44.6.7).

nodes.title: Theorem on formal functions, Grothendieck's existence theorem and algebraization
nodes.statement: (Formal functions, Theorem 30.20.5) For A Noetherian, I ⊂ A an ideal, f: X → Spec A proper and F coherent, H^p(X, F)^∧ ≅ lim_n H^p(X, F/IⁿF), and this is a homeomorphism for the limit topologies. (Grothendieck existence, Theorem 30.27.1) If A is Noetherian and complete with respect to I and X is separated of finite type over A, the completion functor F ↦ (F/IⁿF) is an equivalence from coherent sheaves with support proper over A to coherent formal systems (F_n, F_{n+1}|_{X_n} ≅ F_n) with support proper over A (Remark 30.27.2). (Algebraization, Theorem 30.28.4) A compatible system of schemes X_n over A/Iⁿ with compatible invertible L_n, with X₁ proper and L₁ ample, comes from a proper X with ample L; the ampleness hypothesis cannot be dropped.

nodes.title: First-order deformations of flat modules and flat schemes: obstruction, torsor, automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let (X ⊂ X′) → (S ⊂ S′) be a strict morphism of first-order thickenings of ringed spaces (Definition 91.3.2) with J = Ker(O_{S′} → O_S), f′ flat, and F an O_X-module flat over S. A lift of F to an O_{X′}-module flat over S′ exists iff the class o(F, f^*J ⊗ F, 1) ∈ Ext²(F, f^*J ⊗ F) vanishes; if a lift exists, isomorphism classes of lifts form a principal homogeneous space under Ext¹(F, f^*J ⊗ F), and automorphisms of a lift are given by Ext⁰(F, f^*J ⊗ F) (Lemma 91.6.1). For a first-order thickening of schemes S ⊂ S′ and flat X → S, assuming a flat lift exists, lifts form a torsor under Ext¹(NL_{X/S}, f^*C_{S/S′}) and infinitesimal automorphisms are Ext⁰ (Lemma 91.8.1). Square-zero extensions correspond to Ext¹(NL, G) (Lemma 91.7.4), and a morphism is smooth iff it is locally of finite presentation and formally smooth (Lemma 37.11.7).
hypotheses: Strictness, flatness of f′ and of F over S for the module statement; for schemes the existence of a lift is assumed.

No existence/obstruction statement for deformations of schemes was found; the proof of Lemma 91.7.1(2) is omitted, and Remark 91.7.9 only notes that the relevant maps are close to forming a distinguished triangle.

nodes.title: Modifications, alterations, Lipman's resolution criterion and de Jong's alteration theorems
nodes.statement: A modification is a proper birational morphism from an integral scheme (Stacks Definition 29.51.11); an alteration is a proper dominant morphism from an integral scheme that is finite over a nonempty open (Definition 29.51.12), as in de Jong except that Stacks does not require Noetherian schemes (de Jong 2.17, 2.20: an alteration is generically étale iff the function field extension is separable, and compositions of alterations are alterations). A resolution is a modification with regular source (Definition 54.14.1); for a two-dimensional integral Noetherian scheme, the existence of an alteration from a regular scheme, of a resolution, and of a resolution by normalized blowups, and finiteness of the normalization with finitely many singular points whose completions are normal, are equivalent (Lipman, Theorem 54.14.5). De Jong Theorem 4.1: for a variety X over a field k and a proper closed subset Z ⊂ X there are an alteration φ₁: X₁ → X and an open immersion X₁ ⊂ X̄₁ with X̄₁ projective and regular such that φ₁⁻¹(Z) together with the boundary is a strict normal crossings divisor in X̄₁; if k is perfect, φ₁ may be chosen generically étale; X̄₁ is smooth and geometrically irreducible over a finite extension of k (Remark 4.2). De Jong Theorem 6.5: for X over a trait S (the spectrum of a complete discrete valuation ring) and a proper closed subset Z containing the special fibre, after a finite extension of traits S₁ → S there are an alteration and a projective X̄₁ with geometrically irreducible generic fibre whose pair is strict semi-stable (6.3). For a smooth projective curve C over the fraction field K of a discrete valuation ring with H⁰ = K, semistable reduction holds after a finite separable extension K′/K (Stacks Theorem 55.18.1).
hypotheses: De Jong's variety convention (2.9) was only partly read; Theorem 6.5 is over a complete DVR; resolution is a theorem only in the named two-dimensional setting of Theorem 54.14.5.
The de Jong copy is an OCR text layer with garbled symbols; only clean fragments are quoted. Proofs of Stacks 54.14.5 and 55.18.1 were not read.
proofSteps: De Jong 4.5–4.10: reduce to k algebraically closed, X quasi-projective (Chow's lemma) and then projective, Z a divisor after blowing up, and X normal.
4.11–4.12: fibre X over P^{d−1} in curves (Lemma 4.11), with connected fibres by Stein factorization.
4.13–4.16: add a divisor meeting each fibre component in at least three smooth points (Lemma 4.13) and make Z a union of sections.
4.17–4.21: obtain a stable pointed curve using level-ℓ moduli (2.24) and extend the rational map after flattening (2.19, Lemma 4.20).
4.22–4.28: apply the induction hypothesis on the base, use the local form uv = t₁⋯t_r (Lemma 3.2) and blow up the singular locus to reach strict normal crossings.
acceptance: Alterations and modifications keep distinct outputs (stage text): alterations allow finite extensions of the function field and are weaker than resolution.

nodes.title: Proper pushforward and flat pullback of cycles respect rational equivalence
nodes.statement: In Situation 42.7.1 (S locally Noetherian and universally catenary with a dimension function δ; integer coefficients), proper pushforward (Definition 42.12.1) and flat pullback (Definition 42.14.1) of cycles preserve rational equivalence (Definition 42.19.1): if p is proper and α ~rat β then p_*α ~rat p_*β (Lemma 42.20.3), and the flat pullback analogue holds (Lemma 42.20.2).

If dim p(W) < k the pushforward is zero.

nodes.title: The key lemma, capping with c₁, Gysin maps and Chern classes
nodes.statement: Key Lemma 42.6.3: for a two-dimensional Noetherian local domain A with fraction field K and f, g ∈ K*, the sum over height-one primes q of ord_{A/q}(∂_{A_q}(f, g)) vanishes. Key formula 42.27.1: for invertible modules L and N with meromorphic sections s and t, c₁(N) ∩ div_L(s) and c₁(L) ∩ div_N(t) differ by an explicit sum of divisors of tame symbols. Consequences: capping with c₁ respects rational equivalence (Lemma 42.28.2) and satisfies p_*(c₁(p^*L) ∩ α) = c₁(L) ∩ p_*α (Lemma 42.26.4); the Gysin map of an effective Cartier divisor (Definition 42.29.1) satisfies i_*i^* = c₁(L) ∩ − (Lemma 42.29.4) and factors through rational equivalence (Lemma 42.30.2); Chern classes are defined via the projective bundle formula (Definitions 42.37.1, 42.38.1); degrees of zero-cycles are defined (Definition 42.41.1); and there is an excess formula c(Z → X, N) ∩ [Y] = c_top(E) ∩ [Z ×_X Y] (Lemma 42.54.5, set-up not read).

nodes.title: Intersection products, the moving lemma and the projection formula
nodes.statement: For X smooth over a field, the Chow Homology chapter defines α · β = Δ^!(α × β), which is associative (§42.62, 42.62.1), with projection formula f_*(α · f^!β) = f_*α · β for f proper between smooth k-schemes (Lemma 42.62.4); with rational coefficients there is a product on CH ⊗ Q for X Noetherian, regular, finite dimensional with affine diagonal (Lemma 42.58.1). The Intersection Theory chapter works over an algebraically closed field: for X nonsingular projective, any cycle α is rationally equivalent to α′ meeting a given β properly (Moving Lemma 43.24.3); proper intersections carry Serre's Tor multiplicities (Lemma 43.13.5, §43.17); the intersection product is well defined on rational equivalence classes (Theorem 43.25.2, §43.26); and for f flat proper between nonsingular varieties with α and f^*β intersecting properly, f_*(α) · β = f_*(α · f^*β) (Lemma 43.22.1). Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch is only stated (§42.66).
